1.pericope_label: The two angels come to Sodom

schools.summary: Gill takes the visitors for two of the three who had been with Abraham at Hebron the same day, and has Lot address them as persons of quality with majesty in their countenances, not knowing them for angels and so entertaining them unawares. Calvin asks why one of the three has disappeared, dismisses the Jewish answer that one came to destroy and the other to preserve since both assisted in the rescue, and explains that Abraham had the peculiar favour of God manifesting himself in his own Son, while to Lot Christ made himself known more obscurely, so that only the two came down. He will not affirm that Lot sat in the gate to receive guests, since Moses gives no cause, and thinks it as likely he had come out to see his sheep folded; he reads the angels' refusal as a test of the holy man's disposition, their pretending it safe to sleep on the highway concealing what they knew of the city and making its wickedness appear the greater.

Henry observes that there was but one good man in Sodom and the messengers soon found him out, which he turns into a rule that wherever we are we should seek out those who live in the fear of God. Lot distinguished himself from his neighbours that night, and he that did not act like the rest must not fare like the rest: he sat in the gate at evening while the rest were tippling, and bowed to the ground before men whose bearing was sober though they came in no state, as if he discerned something divine in them.

Clarke notes that some manuscripts turn the negative into a word meaning to him, and explains the angels' refusal by their knowing the temper of the inhabitants while passing for mere travellers, until Lot's vehemence overcame them; he compares our Lord on the road to Emmaus, who made as though he would go further and then yielded. Wesley agrees that these were two of the three who had been with Abraham.

Ellicott notes that the verse continues the preceding narrative, and reads Lot's sitting in the gate as proof that he had become a citizen, probably after the deliverance from the Elamite invasion; that respect closed his eyes to the sinfulness of the people, and meanwhile intercourse with Abraham had ceased and he had lost his share in the covenant of circumcision. He explains the street as the broad open space of the town, where travellers had to lodge before caravanserais existed.

themes: the two angels came to Sodom at even
Lot sat in the gate of Sodom
why only two came down
we will abide in the street all night

4.pericope_label: The men of the city, and Lot's offer

schools.summary: Gill explains that Lot called them brethren not by family, since the Sodomites came of Ham and he of Shem, nor by religion, but by community of nature and long neighbourhood, using soft language only to win them off their purpose. Calvin calls the single crime a lively picture of the place, their consent diabolical, their lust blind, their cruelty plain in besieging a house in a troop, and infers that they were given up to every audacity in crime; he reads their demand as a pretence, since men who meant what the Greek translators supposed would have spoken coarser language. On Lot going out and shutting the door he finds a rare virtue, but treats the offer of the daughters as a defect mixed with great virtue: destitute of advice Lot devised an unlawful remedy, and should rather have endured a thousand deaths than ward off one evil by another.

Henry says the night's work filled the measure and proved the cry of Sodom no louder than there was cause for, marking first that the wickedness was universal, old and young from every quarter, the old not past it and the young already come up to it, so that either the city had no magistrates or they were themselves aiding and abetting.

Clarke will not describe the crime, saying only that the account justifies the character given of the people in the preceding chapter and that the offence is too bad to describe; on the offer of the daughters he holds that nothing but the sacred light in which eastern nations held the rights of hospitality could palliate it, and even so calls the words not only anxious solicitude but unwarrantable haste. Wesley states the rule flatly, that of two evils we must choose the less, but of two sins neither, nor ever do evil that good may come.

Ellicott renders the Hebrew from the end, meaning either to the last man or from the very end of the town, and observes that either way there were not ten righteous men in Sodom to save it. On the offer of the daughters he grants Ambrose's plea that a smaller sin was substituted for a greater and Chrysostom's that hospitality bound Lot to protect his guests, but answers that fatherhood bound him equally to protect his daughters, and that if men might substitute smaller sins for greater they would have an excuse for every wickedness.

debates.question: Can Lot’s offer of his daughters be defended?

sides.position: no defence, only a palliation from the eastern law of hospitality, and even then it was unwarrantable haste
a real defect mixed with real virtue; he warded off evil with evil and should have died sooner
of two evils choose the less, but of two sins neither
the lesser-of-two-sins plea must be refused outright, since it would excuse every wickedness; fatherhood bound him as much as hospitality

themes: the men of Sodom compassed the house
do not so wickedly, my brethren
behold now, I have two daughters
may a smaller sin be chosen to avoid a greater?

9.pericope_label: The assault repelled, and the men struck blind

schools.summary: Gill takes the blindness for a peculiar stroke, of eye and heart together on Aben Ezra's reading, and observes that the Hebrew word occurs only twice and cannot mean blindness as to every object, since men wholly blind would have groped their way home rather than wearied themselves about Lot's house; had they not been given up to judicial blindness such a stroke might have convinced them, whereas they pressed on the harder. Calvin finds the indomitable haughtiness of the people in every word of their answer, notes that Moses still calls the rescuers men though they were not, and takes from the moment a rule about timing, that the Lord may seem regardless while the faithful are in conflict but stretches out his hand at the critical moment; he also sees an exchange in the door Lot had shut for his guests and through which they now receive him.

Clarke infers from their taunt that Lot's sitting in the gate may after all mark a magistrate's place, and sets out two readings of the blindness without preferring either, that the angels deprived them of the regular use of sight or brought on a darkness so deep the door could not be found. Wesley asks only what the stroke was for, and answers that it was to put an end to the attempt and to be an earnest of their utter ruin the next day.

Ellicott sharpens the taunt from the Hebrew, where the one came to sojourn implies a great concession in letting Lot live inside the walls, and he will needs be a judge stands as is ever acting as a judge, implying that Lot had reproved them before. On the blindness he argues that actual blindness is not meant in either place where the word occurs, since blinded men would have fled or groped until they found the door, and an army of blind men could not have been led from Dothan to Samaria; the word means a disturbance of vision in which the eye is not in proper connection with the brain, so the men seemed always about to reach the door and always failed, as they supposed through one another's fault.

debates.question: What kind of blindness fell on the men at the door?

sides.position: a peculiar stroke of eye and heart, blinding them only as to the thing they were intent upon
either a loss of sight or an enveloping darkness — the sources allow both and neither is preferred
not blindness at all but a disturbance of vision, the men unaware anything had happened to them

themes: this one fellow came in to sojourn
they pressed sore upon the man, even Lot
they smote them with blindness
what the blindness was

12.pericope_label: The warning, and the sons-in-law who mocked

schools.summary: Gill marks that once Lot was drawn back inside the visitors began to make themselves known and to tell their errand. Calvin thinks the timing deliberate, and reads the cry of the city being waxen great as a statement about accumulation rather than a single offence, God being provoked not by one act but, after long forbearance, almost compelled by an immense mass of crimes; the more sins men heap together, the nearer their wickedness comes to God to cry for vengeance. He also defends at length the claim that angels are ministers of wrath as well as of grace, holding that God sets his elect angels over the judgments he carries out by means of the reprobate, since devils yield no voluntary obedience but are reluctantly compelled to serve as his executioners.

Henry reads the question whether Lot has any besides in the city as both a command and a favour: the command that he do all he could for those about him, snatching them as brands out of the fire, and the favour in the terms, since the angels do not ask whether he knows any righteous men in Sodom, knowing there were none, but only what kindred he has, so that righteous or unrighteous they might be saved with him. He observes that bad people often fare better in this world for their good relations' sake, and that the holy angels are ministers of God's wrath as well as of his mercy, in which sense the good angels become evil angels.

Clarke works out from the grammar that there were two sons-in-law, the word being singular here and plural in the next verse, and that they were betrothed rather than married, since the daughters are called women who had not known man; reckoned part of the household they were entitled to the offer of protection, but treated the warning as a ridiculous tale and doubtless perished notwithstanding the grace sincerely offered them. Wesley follows Henry on the angels as ministers of wrath.

Ellicott reads the participle as the takers of his daughters, which is why Ewald and Tuch render it of men still only to marry them, though he keeps the traditional sense and finds it confirmed by the next verse, where the two daughters are those found with Lot, implying that he had others besides; on the reception Lot met he notes that the Hebrew is as one laughing, that is, not in earnest.

themes: hast thou here any besides?
the cry of them is waxen great
angels as ministers of wrath
he seemed as one that mocked

15.pericope_label: The lingering, and the hand laid on him

schools.summary: Gill canvasses three reasons for the delay, that Lot was loath to leave his goods, or waiting for his sons-in-law, or praying the city might be spared, but prefers a fourth, that he was so filled with horror at the coming judgments that he stood stupefied with no power to stir. Calvin, having praised Lot's faith, says Moses shows something human still adhered to him: he saw himself going into exile and doubted what would become of a fugitive, failing to consider that he must act like men in a shipwreck who cast their cargo into the sea to come safe into port. Calvin finds the tardiness wonderful, since no words could move him until he was dragged out by the hand; where Christ said the spirit is willing but the flesh weak, here a worse fault appears, the flesh so repressing the spirit's alacrity that it can scarcely creep along.

Clarke supposes Lot still pressing useless entreaties on the family who would not come, and says the angels pulled them away by main force, the Lord being merciful, or they had perished in their lingering as the others perished in their gainsaying; he takes the charge word by word and finds every one emphatic, the danger imminent, a single look back possibly fatal, the plain to be destroyed as well as the city, and the mountain appointed as a refuge. Wesley draws the comfort out: Lot did not make a jest of the warning as his sons-in-law had, but he did not make the haste the case required, and if God had not been merciful to us, our lingering had been our ruin.

Ellicott notes that Lot had the whole night to prepare and spent part of it on the errand to his sons-in-law, says flatly that he clung to his wealth and could not make up his mind to leave it, renders the clause in Jehovah's pity for him, and gives the word behind consumed as swept away. Keil and Delitzsch note that the plural gives way to a singular when the charge is spoken, which sits awkwardly with referring it to one of the two angels since Lot answers him by the name of God, and identify the mountain as the range afterwards called the mountains of Moab.

themes: lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city
while he lingered
the Lord being merciful unto him
escape for thy life, look not behind thee

schools.summary: Gill notices that Lot speaks as though three were present though he addresses only one, and explains the Hebrew behind I have accepted thee as I have lifted up thy face, an allusion to the eastern custom by which a man prostrated himself before his superior and was then bidden raise his face and stand, the token that his suit was granted; he identifies the town as Bela, afterwards Zoar, and weighs the distances from Sodom. Calvin infers from Lot addressing one that he did not rely on the angels at all, using their presence only as a mirror in which the face of God might be contemplated, and approves his rehearsing the mercy already shown as a way of gaining confidence to ask more. The request itself he will not excuse: God assigned a mountain and Lot chose a city, and those who treat the words as a model of prayer are mistaken, since our prayers are faulty so far as they are not founded on the word.

Clarke explains I cannot escape to the mountain as a miscalculation made under pressure, Lot thinking there was not time enough and forgetting that God gives no command impossible to fulfil, though the hurry of his mind will at once account for and excuse so gross an oversight; on the plea that the town was a little one he offers two motives, that Lot wanted it for an inheritance and urged its smallness to get his request granted, or supposed that being little it was less depraved and not yet ripe for punishment, which Clarke thinks probably the case. Wesley draws the moral from the reason given for the delay, that the very presence of good men in a place helps to keep off judgments.
Ellicott renders the following clause literally, lest the evil overtake me, meaning the threatened calamity itself rather than any mishap on the road.

themes: oh, not so, my Lord
this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one
is Lot’s prayer a model or a fault?

23.pericope_label: Fire and brimstone from the Lord

schools.summary: Gill makes the sunrise fix both the hour of Lot's entering Zoar and of Sodom's burning, and takes the fine morning as evidence that what followed did not proceed from natural causes; he supposes an earthquake accompanied the fiery tempest, notes that Strabo attributes the lake to earthquakes and hot bituminous waters without mentioning fire from heaven, and observes that the bitumen pits would have made the shower burn the fiercer. Calvin explains the doubled name as emphasis: God did not cause it to rain in the ordinary course of nature but, as with a stretched-out hand, openly fulminated in a manner to which he was not accustomed, nor was it his will that the cities be simply swallowed by an earthquake. He remarks too that Moses relates the destruction succinctly, reciting a judgment no words would be vehement enough to describe and leaving it to the reader's meditation.

Henry marks the arithmetic of the rescue, that though there were not ten righteous men in Sodom for whose sake it might be spared, the one righteous man among them delivered his own soul, and that the married daughters perished with their unbelieving husbands while those who stayed were preserved.

Clarke reports that many of the primitive fathers and several modern divines read the doubled name as the Son raining from the Father, concedes that two persons named Jehovah in one verse is strange and curious, and yet will not build on it, since the doctrine is established elsewhere and it is better not to use proofs which themselves require proof; on the lake he clears away the legends of the stone that will not sink, the wind that cannot ruffle it and the fruit that turns to ashes, calling them exaggerations or fictions of superstitious monks and of travellers who knew readers delight in the marvellous. Wesley takes the doubled name for God the Son raining from God the Father, since the Father has committed all judgment to the Son.

Ellicott reckons that Lot, starting at dawn, had an hour for his flight, traces the Trinitarian reading of the doubled name to the Council of Sirmium and prefers Calvin's account that the repetition emphasises whose act it was, and grants that natural agencies were used while insisting this does not diminish the event, since a catastrophe of nature became miraculous by its circumstances, and we lose the benefit of Scripture's teaching if we suppose the events recorded there differed in kind from those that happen now.

debates.question: Does “the Lord rained … from the Lord” prove a distinction of Persons?

sides.position: yes; God the Son raining from God the Father, all judgment being committed to the Son
many so read it and the circumstance is strange, but it is not plainly indicated here and the doctrine should not rest on it
no; the repetition is emphatic, marking that the act was Jehovah’s own and no natural event

the Lord rained from the Lord

26.pericope_label: Lot's wife, and Abraham looking toward Sodom

schools.summary: Gill notes that she walked behind Lot, his back toward her, which was itself a temptation, and passes on the Targums' guesses that she wished to see the end of her father's house or whether married daughters followed. Calvin does not explain the manner of her change but defends the fact against those who ridicule it as no likelier than Ovid's metamorphoses: if God made men out of nothing, why may he not reduce them to nothing, and if that be granted, why not turn them into stones? The philosophers who deride it see miracles as great daily in nature. On Abraham he denies that he came because he doubted; persuaded already that the angel had not spoken in vain, he sought confirmation by sight, useful to himself and to posterity.

Henry breaks the act into five faults: she disobeyed an express command, sinning after the similitude of Adam's transgression; unbelief lay at the bottom, since she thought herself still safe in Sodom; she looked back on her neighbours with more concern than was fit; she hankered after her goods, the fault Christ fastens on; and the look showed an inclination to go back, which is why our Saviour makes it a warning against apostasy. He reads Abraham's return to the place as the sequel to prayer, since when we have prayed we must look after our prayers, directing prayer as a letter and then looking for an answer, and distinguishes the two backward looks, Abraham adoring the divine severity where Lot's wife tacitly reflected on it.

Clarke sets out three opinions on her change without endorsing any, that she was turned by miracle into rock salt keeping the human figure, that she was struck by lightning and enveloped in bituminous matter which afterwards resisted air and wet, or that she was consumed in the burning of the plain and the record itself is the memorial; he remarks that Scripture says little and commentators have made the account long by their glosses, and imagines Abraham's astonishment at finding God could not discover ten righteous persons in four cities. Wesley keeps Henry's last two heads.

Keil and Delitzsch hold she was not turned into anything but killed by the sulphureous vapour and afterwards encrusted with salt, noting that objects near the Dead Sea are still quickly crusted over, so that what Christ refers to may be understood without supposing a miracle. Ellicott prefers a third mechanism, that the earthquake heaped up the rock salt lying in strata about the sea and she was caught in the convulsion, leaving the salt hill as her memorial; he explains why Abraham's early start was needed, the place lying some miles off.

debates.question: How did Lot’s wife become a pillar of salt?

sides.position: three opinions are possible — a miraculous change, a lightning stroke with bituminous encrustation, or simple consumption in the fire — and none is preferred
killed by sulphureous vapour and afterwards encrusted with salt, so that no miracle need be supposed
entangled in an earthquake that heaped up the rock salt, leaving the salt hill as her monument
the manner is not explained; the fact is to be defended against those who find it incredible

remember Lot’s wife
Abraham gat up early to the place where he stood
the smoke of the country as the smoke of a furnace

schools.summary: Gill attends to which daughter speaks, the firstborn being the elder of these two, though daughters married in Sodom were probably older still, and reports Aben Ezra's suggestion that Lot had an earlier wife who died; the proposal comes from the elder as the bolder, with more authority and greater power to persuade. Calvin takes the episode as proof that what men contrive by rash counsels of carnal reason never prospers, since temerity often seems successful at first but the Lord at length curses whatever is undertaken without his approval, and Isaiah's woe is fulfilled against those who begin a work and not by the Spirit of the Lord: commanded to the mountain, Lot chose Zoar, and having been granted Zoar he repents and trembles at a destruction hastening on a place so near Sodom.

Henry offers three reasons why Lot durst not stay in Zoar, that he was conscious it was a refuge of his own choosing in which he had prescribed to God, or found it as wicked as Sodom, or watched the waters that after the conflagration began to overflow the plain and by degrees made the Dead Sea; from which he draws the rule that shelters of our own choosing, in which we do not follow God, commonly prove uneasy to us. He finds it strange that Lot did not return to Abraham, who had twice been the means of his safety, and answers that some good men are not wise enough to know what is best for themselves.

Clarke says foolish man ever prefers his own wisdom to his Maker's, it having been wrong at first not to go to the mountain and wrong next to leave the town after God had promised it should be spared, and adds what governs the rest of the chapter, that had Lot stayed at Zoar the shameful transaction afterwards recorded would probably never have happened; on the daughters' reasoning he explains that our father is old means he was not likely to marry again, and that they would have thought a marriage in Zoar dangerous and criminal, that town having been devoted to destruction and spared only at their father's asking. Wesley turns the cave into a warning of what men bring themselves to who forsake the communion of saints for secular advantage.

Keil and Delitzsch place the cave in the Moabitish mountains among caves in which the limestone rocks abound, and mark the limits of the daughters' ignorance, that they did not imagine the whole race had perished in the vale of Siddim but feared no man would link himself with them. Ellicott sets the contrast plainly, the patriarch whose wealth was once so great that he and Abraham could not dwell together being now content with a miserable home in a cavern.

themes: he feared to dwell in Zoar
he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters
there is not a man in the earth to come in unto us

32.pericope_label: The daughters of Lot, and the birth of Moab and Ammon

schools.summary: Gill supposes the wine was part of the provision carried out of Zoar, and refuses the plea that Lot did not know its strength, since he must have known it as well as his daughters, who plainly did, and though he may have drunk more freely to drown his grief this will not excuse drinking to excess; that the same thing happened a second night he takes for the aggravation of the whole business, since Lot ought to have been on his guard. On the names he reports the derivations offered for Moab, from a phrase meaning of the father, so that the elder daughter left the fact in her son's name for all time. Calvin holds that because his drunkenness was the cause of his sin, Lot's guilt is diminished but not annulled, and suspects God struck him with a spirit of stupor beyond what wine alone would do; he is severe on those who make Lot the protector of their own wickedness, and makes the second night a lesson about resisting first beginnings, noting that Lot lived chaste as an angel among the Sodomites and was besieged with new pitfalls as soon as he was safe on the mountain.

Clarke argues the most favourable construction the case will bear, on four grounds: that the daughters do not appear to have acted from any base or sensual desire, that they may have thought marriage into another family criminal, that they may have supposed no other way was left of preserving the family, and that they expected their father to refuse as profane what they judged necessary. He thinks Lot himself in many respects excusable, since he had no accurate knowledge of what happened on either night and might well have judged some servant from Zoar had been in his bed, and thinks him deceived in the wine as well, either not knowing its strength after a life among flocks or being given wine of more than usual power.

Ellicott concedes less than Clarke, allowing that the wish to preserve seed was a very strong feeling in ancient times and affords the sole excuse for the revolting conduct of these women, while calling the degradation of Lot and his family the most painful part of the story, which ends in his intense shame. Keil and Delitzsch note only what the text says, that the one son became father of the Moabites and the other of the children of Ammon, and remained so to the day the words were written.

debates.question: How far are Lot and his daughters chargeable?

sides.position: both are largely excusable — the daughters acted from no sensual motive, and Lot knew nothing of either night and was deceived in the wine
the plea of ignorance fails, since Lot knew the strength of wine as well as his daughters did
his guilt is diminished but not annulled, drunkenness being the cause of the sin
the ancient desire for seed is the sole excuse for the women, and the episode is Lot’s utter degradation
